description: CAIR analysed a 2019 FBI watchlist copy leaked after a regional air carrier accidentally posted it - over 1.5 million entries. The top 50 most frequently occurring names were all Muslim names, and CAIR estimated over 1.47 million entries, more than 98%, regarded Muslims. A separate analysis of the same leak found more than 10% of entries - 174,202 of 1,566,062 - contain 'MUHAMMAD' in the first or last name field.
energy_note: A million and a half names, and the top fifty are all Muslim.
source_name: CAIR analysis of leaked 2019 TSDB copy
notes: HONEST CAVEAT: this is advocacy-organisation analysis of a leaked file, not official data. It is the best available because no official demographic breakdown is published.

aspect: Why name-matching hits this group hardest
description: Screening is name-based, so people not on the list who have names resembling listed ones get misidentified. The effect is pronounced for travellers with common surnames and from backgrounds where name similarity is more likely - which describes Arabic naming conventions precisely.
energy_note: Flagged for having a common name in the wrong language.

aspect: SSSS, and what it costs each time
description: Secondary Security Screening Selection printed on a boarding pass means the passenger and all their belongings are searched. Time in secondary can run to several hours, depending partly on how easily it can be verified that the person is not the one on the list.
money_note: Missed connections, rebooked flights, per occurrence.
energy_note: Four hours, every flight, for years.

aspect: The false-positive volume was large enough for DHS to concede it
description: A then-DHS Secretary cited one major US airline recording 9,000 false positives. DHS has acknowledged that people mistakenly listed or misidentified can face consequences 'ranging from inconvenience and delay to loss of liberty'.
energy_note: Nine thousand wrong flags, at one airline.

aspect: HONEST GAP - there is no published per-ethnicity selection rate
description: TSA does not publish an SSSS selection rate broken down by ethnicity or national origin. The claim that Palestinians are selected at an unusually high rate is supported by the list's composition and by consistent community reporting, not by an official statistic, because that statistic does not exist.
energy_note: Everyone knows the rate. Nobody publishes it.
